'''''Yucca filamentosa''''',<ref>[http://www.botanicus.org/page/358338 Linnaeus, Species Plantarum 1: 319. 1753.]</ref> '''Adam's needle and thread''',<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/19164/i-Yucca-filamentosa-i/Details | title = ''Yucca filamentosa'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 11 March 2019}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Asparagaceae]]<ref>[https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=43140 ''Yucca filamentosa''.] Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS).</ref> [[native plant|native]] to the [[southeastern United States]]. Growing to {{convert|3|m|ft|0|abbr=off}} tall, it is an [[evergreen]] shrub valued in horticulture.

==Description==

Usually trunkless, it is [[Basal shoot|multisuckering]] with heads of {{convert|75|cm|0|abbr=off}} long, filamentous, blue-green, strappy [[leaves]]. ''Y. filamentosa'' is readily distinguished from other yucca species by white, thready filaments along the leaf margins.<ref>''The Reader's Digest Gardeners' Encyclopedia of Plants and Flowers''. Reader's Digest Association. Sydney. 1999.</ref> Flower stems up to {{convert|3|m|ft|0|abbr=off}} tall bear masses of pendulous cream flowers in early summer.<ref name="FNA"/>

==Taxonomy==
''Y. filamentosa'' is closely related to ''[[Yucca flaccida|Y. flaccida]]'' and it is possible they should be classified as a single species.<ref name="FNA"/>

===Names===
Its [[common name]]s include '''Adam's needle''', '''common yucca''', '''Spanish bayonet''',<ref name="ns">[http://www.natureserve.org/explorer/servlet/NatureServe?searchName=Yucca+filamentosa ''Yucca filamentosa''.]{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} NatureServe. 2012.</ref> '''bear-grass''', '''needle-palm''', '''silk-grass''', and '''spoon-leaf yucca'''.<ref name="grin">{{GRIN | access-date = 4 January 2018}}</ref> 

==Distribution and habitat==
''Yucca filamentosa'' is only native from Maryland south to Florida and westwards to Louisiana. Inland it is native to Tennessee and West Virginia,<ref name="FNA">{{Cite web <!--Deny Citation Bot-->|last1=Hess |first1= William J. |last2=Robbins |first2=R. Laurie |date=5 November 2020 |orig-date=In print 2002 |url=https://floranorthamerica.org/Yucca_filamentosa |title=''Yucca filamentosa'' |website=[[Flora of North America]] |page=433 |language=en-us |isbn=978-0-19-515208-1 |oclc=65199362 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250210193820/https://floranorthamerica.org/Yucca_filamentosa |archive-date=10 February 2025 |access-date=11 December 2025}}</ref> but is introduced to Kentucky.<ref name="POWO">{{cite POWO |id=325008-2 |title=''Yucca filamentosa'' L. |access-date=11 December 2025}}</ref> It has also an introduced plant in New York and Massachusetts and is also reported in France, Germany, Italy, Albania, Hungary, Romania, and Turkey.<ref name="POWO" />

In its native environment, ''Yucca filamentosa'' is most commonly found in sunny open areas in sandy soils, especially in beach scrub and sand dunes, but also in fields, barrens, and rocky slopes, though it grows well also in silt or clay soils. Normally ''Yucca filamentosa'' will spread horizontally across open sunny and dry areas, creating a dense thicket of sword like foliage. ''Yucca filamentosa'' is hardy to USDA zone 5 to 12.

==Ecology==
The plants are [[pollinated]] by the yucca moth ''[[Tegeticula yuccasella]]''.<ref>Marr, D. L., et al. (2000). [https://web.archive.org/web/20141216063721/http://www.amjbot.org/content/87/5/670.long Pollen dispersal in ''Yucca filamentosa'' (Agavaceae): the paradox of self-pollination behavior by ''Tegeticula yuccasella'' (Prodoxidae).] ''American Journal of Botany'' 87(5), 670-77.</ref><ref>Wunderlin, R. P. 1998. Guide to the Vascular Plants of Florida i–x, 1–806. University Press of Florida, Gainesville.</ref> Other moth species, such as ''[[Tegeticula intermedia]]'', also use this yucca as a host plant to lay their eggs.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://tolweb.org/Tegeticula_intermedia/12474|title=Tegeticula intermedia|website=tolweb.org|access-date=2017-11-16}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Y. filamentosa'' is widely cultivated in mild [[temperateness|temperate]] and subtropical climates. A fairly compact species, it nevertheless presents a striking appearance with its sword-like leaves and dramatic flowerheads. It is naturally a focal point in the landscape, also providing a tropical touch in temperate gardens. It needs full sun and a well-drained soil, preferring an acid or slightly alkaline [[Soil pH|pH]] range of 5.5 to 7.5. It develops a large, fleshy, white taproot with deep lateral roots. Once planted and established, it is difficult to remove, as the roots keep sending up new shoots for many years. It is normally [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] down to {{convert|-29|C|F|abbr=on}}, or [[U.S. Department of Agriculture]] (USDA) [[hardiness zone]]s of 5 to 9: UK H7).

===Cultivars===
'Bright Edge', a dwarf [[cultivar]] with yellow-margined foliage and creamy flowers tinged with green, has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|title=RHS Plant Selector - ''Yucca filamentosa'' 'Bright Edge' | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/44109/Yucca-filamentosa-Bright-Edge-(v)/Details | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 107 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 18 February 2019}}</ref> 'Color Guard', with broad yellow  stripes all year plus red stripes in the winter, has also won the award.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/168496/Yucca-filamentosa-Color-Guard-(v)/Details | title = ''Yucca filamentosa'' 'Color Guard' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 11 March 2019}}</ref> 

Other cultivars include:
* 'Golden Sword' - with yellow centered leaves and green margins.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dirr |first=Michael A. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OCVFA1hm8qUC&pg=PA886 |title=Dirr's Encyclopedia of Trees and Shrubs |date=2011-10-18 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0-88192-901-0 |language=en}}</ref>
* 'Ivory Tower' - with larger, branched inflorescence.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Flint |first=Harrison L. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Q1_fAywb_bkC&pg=PA745 |title=Landscape Plants for Eastern North America: Exclusive of Florida and the Immediate Gulf Coast |date=1997-04-09 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-471-59919-7 |language=en}}</ref>

==Uses==
Once the seeds have been removed, the fruits can be cooked and eaten. The large flower petals can also be eaten in salads.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-date=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=616}}</ref>

The leaves, stems and roots of this plant can be used to [[Fish toxins|stun fish]].<ref>{{cite book | last = Duffy | first = K. | title = Harvesting Nature's Bounty, Second Edition | publisher = Bookman Pub | location = City | year = 2004 | isbn = 1-59453-294-X }}</ref> The [[Cherokee]] used it for this purpose.<ref>[http://naeb.brit.org/uses/44057/''Yucca filamentosa''.] Native American Ethnobotany DB. University of Michigan, Dearborn.</ref>
